import pytest
from inflection import (
    camelize,
    dasherize,
    humanize,
    ordinal,
    ordinalize,
    parameterize,
    pluralize,
    singularize,
    tableize,
    titleize,
    transliterate,
    underscore,
)


def test_titleize__hyphenated_words():
    assert titleize("x-men: the last stand") == "X Men: The Last Stand"


def test_ordinalize__basic():
    # Typical positive numbers
    assert ordinalize(1) == "1st"
    assert ordinalize(2) == "2nd"
    assert ordinalize(3) == "3rd"
    assert ordinalize(4) == "4th"
    assert ordinalize(11) == "11th"  # teens exception
    assert ordinalize(12) == "12th"
    assert ordinalize(13) == "13th"
    assert ordinalize(21) == "21st"
    assert ordinalize(22) == "22nd"
    assert ordinalize(23) == "23rd"
    assert ordinalize(100) == "100th"
    assert ordinalize(101) == "101st"
    assert ordinalize(102) == "102nd"
    assert ordinalize(103) == "103rd"
    assert ordinalize(1002) == "1002nd"
    assert ordinalize(1003) == "1003rd"
    # Negative numbers
    assert ordinalize(-11) == "-11th"
    assert ordinalize(-1021) == "-1021st"
    assert ordinalize(-1) == "-1st"
    assert ordinalize(-2) == "-2nd"
    assert ordinalize(-3) == "-3rd"
    assert ordinalize(-4) == "-4th"

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "number, expected_suffix",
    [
        # Docstring examples
        (1, "st"),
        (2, "nd"),
        (1002, "nd"),
        (1003, "rd"),
        (-11, "th"),
        (-1021, "st"),

        # Additional cases for comprehensive coverage
        # Covers 'rd' case explicitly (number % 10 == 3)
        (3, "rd"),
        # Covers default 'th' from get() (number % 10 == 4)
        (4, "th"),
        # Covers default 'th' from get() (number % 10 == 0)
        (10, "th"),
        # Covers number % 100 == 12
        (12, "th"),
        # Covers number % 100 == 13
        (13, "th"),
        # Covers default 'th' from get() for a larger number ending in 0
        (100, "th"),
        # Covers 'st' for a number > 100 not ending in 11
        (101, "st"),
        # Covers 'nd' for a number > 100 not ending in 12
        (102, "nd"),
        # Covers 'rd' for a number > 100 not ending in 13
        (103, "rd"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 1, not 11
        (-1, "st"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 2, not 12
        (-2, "nd"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 3, not 13
        (-3, "rd"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 4
        (-4, "th"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 0
        (-10, "th"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 12
        (-12, "th"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 13
        (-13, "th"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 100
        (-100, "th"),
        # Covers abs() with negative input ending in 101
        (-101, "st"),
    ],
)
def test_ordinal__basic(number, expected_suffix):
    """
    Test the ordinal function with a variety of typical valid integer inputs,
    including positive, negative, and edge cases around 11, 12, 13, and 1, 2, 3.
    This test also ensures coverage of all specified lines.
    """
    assert ordinal(number) == expected_suffix

def test_parameterize__strip_bug():
    """
    The regex that strips leading and trailing separators must only remove those
    separators, not the entire string. With a default separator '-', an input that
    results in leading and trailing hyphens after the replacement step should be
    stripped to the inner word only. A buggy regex that matches the whole string
    would return an empty string, causing this test to fail.
    """
    input_str = " -Hello- "
    # After transliteration and replacement:
    #   spaces -> '-', yielding "-Hello-"
    #   collapse multiple separators (none needed)
    #   strip leading/trailing '-' -> "Hello"
    #   lowercased -> "hello"
    assert parameterize(input_str, separator="-") == "hello"


def test_parameterize__sep_empty_bug():
    """
    When separator is an empty string, the function should *not* invoke the
    leading/trailing separator removal regex. The expected result is the
    transliterated string with non‑alphanumeric characters removed and lower‑cased.
    A buggy implementation that runs the regex and replaces the whole result with
    'XX' would cause this test to fail.
    """
    input_str = "Hello World"
    # transliterate leaves the string unchanged (ASCII only)
    # non‑alphanumeric chars (space) are removed because separator == ''
    # => "HelloWorld" -> lowercased => "helloworld"
    assert parameterize(input_str, separator="") == "helloworld"
